description: Everything in the Wolfram Language is an expression of the form head[args], and the evaluator rewrites expressions until nothing changes. This category covers the constructs that control when evaluation happens, the functions that inspect and manipulate expression structure, symbol attributes and contexts, package and option machinery, and the tracing tools used to understand what the evaluator did.

tools.name: Hold
tools.description: Keeps an expression unevaluated, wrapping it so it can be stored, inspected or transformed before being released. Hold has attribute HoldAll, so nothing inside it evaluates. It is the standard container for code treated as data, and ReleaseHold evaluates the contents when you are ready.
tools.example:
Hold[1 + 1]
ReleaseHold[Hold[1 + 1]]
Hold[Print["a"]; Print["b"]]
Hold[x^2] /. x -> 3
Extract[{1 + 1, 2 + 2}, 1, Hold]
tools.notes: Rules applied to a held expression act on the unevaluated form, which makes Hold the basis of code transformation. Use HoldComplete when even upvalues and sequence splicing must be suppressed.

tools.name: HoldForm
tools.description: Keeps an expression unevaluated but prints it without showing any wrapper, which makes it the tool for displaying unevaluated formulas. It behaves exactly like Hold for evaluation purposes and is what Trace and message formatting use internally. ReleaseHold removes it and evaluates the contents.
tools.example:
HoldForm[2 + 2]
HoldForm[Integrate[x^2, x]] == Integrate[x^2, x]
ReleaseHold[HoldForm[2^10]]
Row[{HoldForm[Sum[i, {i, n}]], " = ", Sum[i, {i, n}]}]

tools.name: HoldComplete
tools.description: Holds an expression absolutely, blocking not just evaluation of the arguments but also upvalue application and Sequence splicing that Hold still allows. It is the safe container when an expression must be preserved byte for byte, for instance when building code generators. ReleaseHold releases it in the same way as Hold.
tools.example:
Hold[Sequence[1, 2]]
HoldComplete[Sequence[1, 2]]
HoldComplete[Evaluate[1 + 1]]
ReleaseHold[HoldComplete[2 + 3]]
tools.notes: Evaluate has no effect inside HoldComplete, which is the key difference from Hold.

tools.name: ReleaseHold
tools.description: Removes Hold, HoldForm, HoldPattern and HoldComplete wrappers wherever they appear in an expression and lets the contents evaluate. It only strips wrappers at the positions where they occur, so nested holds may need repeated application. It is the counterpart of the Hold family.
tools.example:
ReleaseHold[Hold[1 + 1]]
ReleaseHold[{Hold[2^3], Hold[4 + 5]}]
ReleaseHold[Hold[Hold[1 + 1]]]
ReleaseHold[HoldForm[Sqrt[16]]]

tools.name: Evaluate
tools.description: Forces an argument to be evaluated even when the enclosing function has a Hold attribute. It is essential when passing a computed list of expressions to Plot, Manipulate, Do or any HoldAll function that would otherwise treat it literally. Evaluate works only at the top level of the argument it wraps.
tools.notes: Plotting a list held in a variable without Evaluate is a classic source of slow or blank plots, because Plot then re-evaluates the whole list at every sample point.

tools.name: Unevaluated
tools.description: Passes an argument to a function without evaluating it, while the wrapper itself disappears when the function receives it. Unlike Hold it leaves no trace in the argument, so the function sees exactly the raw expression. It is the way to hand unevaluated input to a function that does not have a Hold attribute.
tools.example:
Length[Unevaluated[1 + 2 + 3]]
Length[1 + 2 + 3]
Attributes[Unevaluated]
Head[Unevaluated[2 + 2]]
tools.notes: Unevaluated is stripped by the evaluator exactly once, at the point where the enclosing function is applied; nested uses behave differently from Hold.

tools.name: Defer
tools.description: Holds an expression and displays it unevaluated, but the displayed output can be edited and evaluated as input in a notebook. It is the tool for generating input cells programmatically and for showing a computation the user is meant to run. Unlike HoldForm the result is intended to be re-entered.
tools.example:
Defer[Integrate[x^2, x]]
CellPrint[ExpressionCell[Defer[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}]], "Input"]]
Defer[2 + 2]

tools.name: Head
tools.description: Gives the head of an expression, which is the function part of head[args] and the type indicator for atoms. Head[5] is Integer, Head["s"] is String, Head[{1,2}] is List. A second argument supplies a value to return for atomic expressions.
tools.example:
Head[f[x, y]]
Head[{1, 2, 3}]
Head[5]
Head[5.]
Head[a + b]
tools.notes: Head is what _h patterns test against, which is why _Real does not match an integer. Use NumericQ for a value-based numeric test rather than a head test.

tools.name: Level
tools.description: Gives the list of subexpressions at a specified level of an expression. Level 1 is the immediate arguments, level -1 the atoms, and {m, n} a range of levels. It is the general traversal primitive underlying the level specifications used by Map, Cases, Position and Apply.
tools.example:
Level[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, 1]
Level[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, 2]
Level[f[g[x], h[y]], {-1}]
Level[a + b c, {1}]
Level[expr, {0, Infinity}]

tools.name: Depth
tools.description: Gives the maximum number of index levels needed to reach any part of an expression, counting the top level as 1. An atom has depth 1 and a flat list depth 2. It is a quick way to check how deeply nested a structure is, complementing Dimensions for non-rectangular data.
tools.example:
Depth[5]
Depth[{1, 2, 3}]
Depth[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Depth[f[g[h[x]]]]
ArrayDepth[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
tools.notes: ArrayDepth gives the number of rectangular levels only, which is the meaningful measure for tensors.

tools.name: FullForm
tools.description: Displays an expression in its underlying internal representation, with no special input or output syntax. It reveals that {a, b} is List[a, b], that a/b is Times[a, Power[b, -1]] and that 2x is Times[2, x]. It is the single most useful diagnostic when a pattern or rule is not matching as expected.
tools.example:
FullForm[{1, 2}]
FullForm[a/b]
FullForm[x^2 + 1]
FullForm[Hold[2 + 2]]
FullForm[-x]
tools.notes: Use it together with Hold when the expression would otherwise evaluate: FullForm[Hold[a/b]] shows the structure before evaluation.

tools.name: TreeForm
tools.description: Displays an expression as a graphical tree of heads and arguments, which makes deeply nested structure much easier to read than FullForm. A depth argument limits how many levels are drawn. It is primarily a teaching and debugging aid.
tools.example:
TreeForm[a + b c]
TreeForm[{1, {2, 3}, {4, {5}}}]
TreeForm[x^2 + Sin[y], 2]
ExpressionTree[a + b c]
tools.notes: ExpressionTree (Wolfram Language 13.1 and later) builds a computable Tree object from an expression, which can be queried and mapped over.

tools.name: InputForm
tools.description: Displays an expression in a plain linear form that can be typed back in as valid input. It is the right output form when writing results to a file, sending them to another program, or comparing text representations. ToString[expr, InputForm] produces the same text as a string.
tools.example:
InputForm[Sqrt[2]/3]
InputForm[N[Pi, 20]]
ToString[{1, 2, 3}, InputForm]
OutputForm[x/y]
InputForm["text"]
tools.notes: OutputForm and StandardForm are for display; only InputForm is guaranteed to round-trip through ToExpression.

tools.name: Attributes
tools.description: Gives the list of attributes of a symbol, such as Listable, HoldAll, Orderless, Flat, Protected and NumericFunction. Attributes change how the evaluator treats a function before its definitions are even consulted. Assigning to Attributes[f] replaces the whole attribute list.
tools.example:
Attributes[Plus]
Attributes[Sin]
Attributes[Hold]
Attributes[f] = {Listable, Protected};
Attributes[Set]

tools.name: SetAttributes
tools.description: Adds one or more attributes to a symbol without disturbing the others. It is how user functions are made Listable so they thread over lists, or HoldAll so they receive unevaluated arguments. ClearAttributes removes attributes again.
tools.usage:
SetAttributes[f, attr]
SetAttributes[f, {attr1, attr2}]
SetAttributes[{f, g}, attr]
tools.notes: Set attributes before writing definitions where the attribute affects how the left-hand side is interpreted, particularly for Hold* and Orderless.

tools.name: ClearAttributes
tools.description: Removes specified attributes from a symbol, leaving the rest and all definitions intact. It is most often used to remove Protected from a built-in (though Unprotect is the usual spelling) or to undo an experimental Listable. Attributes[f] = {} clears them all at once.

tools.name: HoldAll
tools.description: An attribute that stops all arguments of a function from being evaluated before the function's own rules are applied, with HoldFirst and HoldRest holding only some of them. It is what makes control structures such as If, While and Module possible in user code. Inside such a function, use Evaluate or explicit evaluation to process arguments when needed.
tools.usage:
SetAttributes[f, HoldAll]
SetAttributes[f, HoldFirst]
SetAttributes[f, HoldRest]
tools.notes: HoldAllComplete additionally blocks upvalues and Sequence splicing, matching what HoldComplete does for a wrapper.

tools.name: Listable
tools.description: An attribute that makes a function automatically thread over lists given as arguments, so f[{1,2,3}] becomes {f[1], f[2], f[3]} without any Map. Nearly all built-in mathematical functions have it, which is why Sin[list] works. For several list arguments they must be the same length and are threaded in parallel.
tools.notes: Listable functions are also automatically parallelized over packed arrays internally, which makes them much faster than an explicit Map.

tools.name: Flat
tools.description: An attribute making a function associative, so nested calls are flattened automatically: f[f[a, b], c] becomes f[a, b, c]. Orderless makes a function commutative by sorting its arguments into canonical order, and OneIdentity affects how single-argument patterns match. Plus and Times carry Flat, Orderless and OneIdentity, which is why their patterns match so flexibly.
tools.usage:
SetAttributes[f, Flat]
SetAttributes[f, Orderless]
SetAttributes[f, {Flat, Orderless, OneIdentity}]
tools.notes: Flat and Orderless make pattern matching much more expensive because many argument groupings must be tried; use them deliberately.

tools.name: Protect
tools.description: Sets the Protected attribute on symbols so their definitions cannot be changed accidentally. All built-in system symbols are protected. Protect accepts string patterns, so Protect["MyPackage`*"] locks a whole context at the end of a package file.
tools.example:
Protect[myFunction];
myFunction[x_] := x
Protect["MyPackage`*"]
MemberQ[Attributes[Sin], Protected]

tools.name: Unprotect
tools.description: Removes the Protected attribute so definitions can be added or changed, which is required before adding rules to built-in symbols. Extending a built-in this way is powerful but risky, since it changes behaviour globally; UpValues on your own symbols are usually the safer approach. Re-protect afterwards to avoid accidental redefinition.
tools.notes: Prefer TagSet (f /: ...) or UpSet to attach behaviour to your own symbol instead of modifying a protected built-in.

tools.name: Symbol
tools.description: Creates or refers to a symbol with a given name supplied as a string, which is how symbols are generated programmatically. The symbol is created in the current context unless the name includes an explicit context. Unique and Module generate fresh guaranteed-unused symbols instead.
tools.example:
Symbol["x"]
Symbol["a" <> ToString[1]]
Table[Symbol["v" <> ToString[i]], {i, 3}]
Unique["temp"]
Symbol["System`Pi"]
tools.notes: Building symbol names dynamically makes code hard to follow and can clash with existing names; an Association keyed by strings is usually a better data structure.

tools.name: SymbolName
tools.description: Gives the short name of a symbol as a string, without its context prefix. It has attribute HoldAll in effect through its usage pattern, so pass the symbol directly. Context[sym] gives the context part, and the two together reconstruct the full name.
tools.example:
SymbolName[x]
SymbolName[Global`myVar]
Context[Sin] <> SymbolName[Sin]
SymbolName /@ {a, b, c}
tools.notes: SymbolName evaluates its argument, so SymbolName[x] after x = 5 fails; wrap in Hold or use Unevaluated when the symbol has a value.

tools.name: Names
tools.description: Gives a list of the names of symbols matching a string pattern, using shell-style metacharacters or a full string pattern. Names["Global`*"] lists everything the user has defined, and Names["*Plot*"] finds built-ins by substring. It is the primary reflection and discovery tool.
tools.example:
Names["Global`*"]
Names["*Transform"]
Length[Names["System`*"]]
Names[RegularExpression["Bessel.*"]]
Names["List*"]
tools.notes: Combine with Information or ?name to inspect what a discovered symbol does, and with Clear["Global`*"] to reset a session.

tools.name: Context
tools.description: Gives the context in which a symbol lives, as a string ending in a backquote, such as "System`" or "Global`". Contexts are the Wolfram Language namespace mechanism: the full name of a symbol is context plus short name. Context[] with no argument gives the current context, the same as $Context.
tools.example:
Context[Sin]
Context[myVariable]
Context[]
$Context
$ContextPath

tools.name: $ContextPath
tools.description: The list of contexts searched when an unqualified symbol name is typed, in order. $Context is the context in which new symbols are created. Shadowing warnings occur when the same short name exists in two contexts on the path; Remove the unwanted one to fix it.
tools.example:
$Context
$ContextPath
Block[{$ContextPath = {"System`"}}, Context[Sin]]
Needs["GraphUtilities`"];
$ContextPath
tools.notes: Needs and Get manage $ContextPath automatically; modifying it by hand is rarely necessary outside package development.

tools.name: BeginPackage
tools.description: Starts a package by setting the context and resetting $ContextPath so only System` and any declared dependencies are visible. Public symbols and their usage messages are declared between BeginPackage and Begin["`Private`"], and EndPackage restores the previous context while adding the new one to $ContextPath. This is the standard structure of every .wl package file.
tools.notes: Declaring the public symbols before Begin["`Private`"] is what makes them visible to users; symbols first mentioned inside the private section stay private.

tools.name: Begin
tools.description: Switches the current context so that new symbols are created there, with End[] restoring the previous one. Inside a package Begin["`Private`"] creates a subcontext for implementation symbols that users should not see. Unlike BeginPackage it does not touch $ContextPath.

tools.name: Needs
tools.description: Loads a package only if its context is not already present, which makes it safe to call repeatedly and is the correct way to declare a dependency. Get (<<) always reloads, which can duplicate definitions and clobber user changes. Needs searches $Path and the installed paclets for the file.
tools.notes: Listing dependencies as the second argument of BeginPackage calls Needs on each one automatically at load time.

tools.name: Get
tools.description: Reads a file and evaluates its contents in the current session, written in shorthand as <<"file". It is used to load packages, .mx dumps and saved definitions, and it returns the value of the last expression in the file. Unlike Needs it always re-reads the file.
tools.example:
Get["C:\\code\\defs.wl"]
<< GeneralUtilities`
Get[FileNameJoin[{NotebookDirectory[], "helpers.wl"}]]
Get["dump.mx"]
tools.notes: Get fails silently in scripts if the file is not on $Path; check with FindFile or use an absolute path built with FileNameJoin.

tools.name: Options
tools.description: Gives the list of default option rules for a symbol, and assigning to Options[f] declares the options a user-defined function accepts. Options[expr, name] extracts the current setting of one option from an expression or object. It is the foundation of the named-option convention used throughout the language.
tools.example:
Options[Plot]
Options[f] = {Tolerance -> 0.001, Method -> Automatic};
Options[f]
Options[Plot, PlotRange]
Options[graphicsObject]

tools.name: OptionValue
tools.description: Retrieves the value of an option inside a function that was defined with an OptionsPattern[] argument, falling back to the declared default when the caller did not supply it. Inside such a definition OptionValue[name] needs no other arguments because the option list is picked up automatically. This is the modern, correct way to read options in user code.
tools.usage:
OptionValue[name]
OptionValue[f, opts, name]
OptionValue[{opts}, name]
tools.notes: OptionValue only works inside a definition whose left-hand side contains OptionsPattern[]; elsewhere use the three-argument form or plain ReplaceAll on the option list.

tools.name: OptionsPattern
tools.description: A pattern object matching any sequence of option rules at the end of a function's arguments, normally written opts : OptionsPattern[]. Combined with Options and OptionValue it gives user functions the same option behaviour as built-ins. It matches zero or more rules, including a nested list of rules.
tools.usage:
f[args, opts : OptionsPattern[]]
OptionsPattern[]
OptionsPattern[{f, g}]
tools.notes: Passing opts straight through to a built-in, as in Plot[..., opts], is the idiomatic way to forward user options.

tools.name: SetOptions
tools.description: Changes the default settings of options for a symbol or an open notebook object for the rest of the session. It is how you set a preferred plot style or working precision once instead of repeating it in every call. It returns the full updated option list.
tools.usage:
SetOptions[f, opt -> val]
SetOptions[f, {opt1 -> v1, opt2 -> v2}]
tools.notes: Global option changes persist for the session and can make later code behave unexpectedly; prefer passing options explicitly in reusable code.

tools.name: Information
tools.description: Gives detailed information about a symbol: usage message, attributes, options and definitions, returned as a formatted object or as data when a property is requested. The shorthand ?name and ??name print the same information in a notebook. It is the main introspection entry point.
tools.example:
Information[Sin]
Information[Sin, "Options"]
Information[Plot, "OptionsNames"]
?Integrate
Information[myFunc, "Usage"]

tools.name: Definition
tools.description: Displays everything currently assigned to a symbol: its own values, down values, up values, attributes, options and defaults. It is the quickest way to see all the definitions of a function you have written, including memoized values. FullDefinition follows through to the symbols used in those definitions as well.
tools.notes: Save["file.wl", f] writes essentially the same content to a file, which is a convenient way to persist definitions.

tools.name: Trace
tools.description: Returns a nested list of all the intermediate expressions produced while evaluating an expression, optionally filtered by a pattern so only matching steps are shown. It is the definitive tool for understanding why an evaluation gave an unexpected result. TracePrint prints the steps as they happen, which works better for long or non-terminating evaluations.
tools.usage:
Trace[expr]
Trace[expr, form]
TracePrint[expr]
TraceScan[f, expr]
tools.example:
Trace[1 + 2 + 3]
Trace[Fibonacci[4], _Plus]
Trace[x = 5; x^2]
TracePrint[2 + 2 + 2]
Trace[mySlowFunc[3], myHelper[_]]
tools.notes: An unfiltered Trace of a real computation produces an enormous result; always supply a pattern such as the name of your own function.

tools.name: Sequence
tools.description: Represents a sequence of arguments that is automatically spliced into the enclosing function call, so f[Sequence[a, b]] becomes f[a, b]. Sequence[] disappears entirely, which makes it the general way to conditionally omit an argument. It is what __ patterns bind to on the right-hand side of a rule.
tools.example:
f[Sequence[a, b], c]
List[1, Sequence[2, 3], 4]
f[x__] := {x};
Plus[Sequence @@ {1, 2, 3}]
Sequence[]
tools.notes: Sequence splices inside any head, unlike Nothing which only vanishes inside List. Hold shows a Sequence unspliced but HoldComplete is needed to preserve it fully.

tools.name: Message
tools.description: Issues a named message defined as symbol::tag, substituting arguments into the `` `1` `` slots of the message text. It is the standard way for user functions to report problems in the same style as built-ins. Quiet suppresses selected messages and Check detects whether any were generated.
tools.usage:
f::tag = "text with `1`";
Message[f::tag, args]
Quiet[expr, {f::tag}]
Check[expr, failexpr]
tools.notes: Messages are also controlled by Off and On, and $MessageList records which ones were generated during the last evaluation.
